ns0:a.ns1:title: G.1 (I.def.1): A point A is that which has no part.
G.2 (I.def.2): A line [ A B ] is a projection of a relationship of two points A, B.
G.3 (I.def.3): The extremities of a segment / A B / are points A, B.
G.4 (I.def.4): A segment / A B / is a portion of a line [ A B ] between two points A, B on the line.
G.5 (I.def.5): A surface is that which has length and breadth only.
G.6 (I.def.6): The extremities of a surface are lines or arcs.
G.7 (I.def.7): A plane surface lies evenly with the lines on itself.
G.8 (I.def.13): A boundary is the extremity of anything.
G.9 (I.def.14): A figure is that which is contained by any boundary or boundaries.

G.10 (I.def.15): A circle ( A B ) is a plane figure contained by one arc defined by a center A and a point B establishing its defining radius / A B /, such that all segments / A B /, / A C /, / A D...
G.11 (I.def.19): Rectilineal figures are contained by segments: trilateral by three, quadrilateral by four, and multilateral by more than four.

G.12 (I.def.20): Of trilateral figures, an equilateral triangle < A B C > has three equal sides, an isosceles triangle < D E F > has two equal sides, and a scalene triangle < G H K > has three uneq...
G.13 (I.post.1): Construct a segment / A B / between any two points A, B.
G.14 (I.def.16): The point A within the circle ( A B ) from which all segments / A B /, / A C / to the arc are equal is called the center of the circle.
G.15 (I.post.3): Construct a circle ( A B ) with center A and defining radius point B.
G.16 (I.cn.1): Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
G.17 (I.1): Construct an equilateral triangle on a given segment.
G.18 (I.post.2): Extend a segment / A B / continuously along a line [ A B ] to / B C /.
G.19 (I.cn.3): If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
G.20 (I.2): Construct at a given point a segment equal to a given segment.
G.21 (I.3): Cut off from the greater of two unequal segments a segment equal to the less.
G.22 (I.def.8): A plane angle is the inclination to one another of two lines or arcs in a plane that meet and do not lie on the same line.
G.23 (I.cn.4): Things / A B /, / D E / that coincide with one another are equal to one another.
G.24 (I.4): Triangles with two sides and the included angle equal are congruent (SAS).
G.25 (I.5): In an isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal, and if the equal sides are extended, the angles under the base are equal.
G.27 (I.7): On the same segment and on the same side, there cannot be constructed two distinct triangles with both pairs of conterminous sides equal.
G.28 (I.8): Triangles with all three corresponding sides equal have their corresponding angles equal (SSS).
G.29 (I.def.9): A rectilineal angle is contained by two segments or lines.
G.30 (I.9): Bisect a given angle.
G.31 (I.10): Bisect a given segment.
G.32 (I.def.10): When a segment standing on a line makes the adjacent angles equal, each of the equal angles is a right angle, and the standing segment is perpendicular to the line.
G.33 (I.11): Construct a segment at right angles to a given line from a given point on it.
G.35 (I.cn.2): If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
G.36 (I.13): A segment standing on a line makes either two right angles or adjacent angles summing to two right angles.
G.37 (I.post.4): All right angles are equal.
G.38 (I.14): If two segments at a point on a line on opposite sides make adjacent angles summing to two right angles, the two segments are collinear.
G.39 (I.15): Intersecting lines make their vertical angles equal.
G.40 (I.cn.5): The whole is greater than the part.
G.41 (I.16): In any triangle, if one side is extended, the exterior angle is greater than either opposite interior angle.
G.42 (I.17): In any triangle, the sum of any two angles is less than two right angles.
G.43 (I.18): In any triangle, the greater side subtends the greater angle.
G.44 (I.19): In any triangle, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.
G.45 (I.20): In any triangle, the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining side.
G.47 (I.22): Construct a triangle from three segments equal to three given segments satisfying the triangle inequality.
G.48 (I.23): Construct on a given line at a given point an angle equal to a given angle.
G.51 (I.26): Triangles with two angles and one corresponding side equal are congruent (ASA / AAS).
G.52 (I.def.23): Parallel lines are lines in the same plane which, extended indefinitely in both directions, do not meet.
G.53 (I.27): If a transversal cutting two lines makes the alternate interior angles equal, the lines are parallel.
G.54 (I.28): If a transversal cutting two lines makes the exterior angle equal to the opposite interior angle, or interior angles on the same side supplementary, the lines are parallel.
G.55 (I.post.5): Two lines intersected by a transversal with interior angles on one side summing to less than two right angles meet on that side.
G.56 (I.29): A transversal cutting parallel lines makes alternate interior angles equal, exterior and opposite interior angles equal, and same-side interior angles supplementary.
G.57 (I.30): Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to one another.
G.58 (I.31): Construct through a given point a line parallel to a given line.
G.59 (I.32): In any triangle, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and the three interior angles sum to two right angles.
G.60 (I.33): Segments joining the endpoints of equal and parallel segments in the same directions are themselves equal and parallel.
G.61 (I.def.17): A diameter of a circle is any segment drawn through the center and terminated in both directions by the arc of the circle; it bisects the circle.
G.62 (I.34): In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal bisects the area.

G.63 (I.def.22): Of quadrilateral figures, a square is equilateral and right-angled; an oblong is right-angled but not equilateral; a rhombus is equilateral but not right-angled; a rhomboid has opp...
G.64 (I.35): Parallelograms on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.65 (I.36): Parallelograms on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.66 (I.37): Triangles on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.67 (I.38): Triangles on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.68 (I.39): Equal triangles on the same base and on the same side lie in the same parallels.
G.70 (I.41): If a parallelogram shares the same base with a triangle and lies in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double the triangle.
G.71 (I.42): Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
G.72 (I.43): In any parallelogram, the complements of the parallelograms about the diagonal are equal in area.
G.73 (I.44): Apply to a given segment, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
G.74 (I.45): Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given polygon.
G.76 (I.def.11): An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle.
G.77 (I.def.12): An acute angle is less than a right angle.
G.78 (I.def.21): A right-angled triangle has a right angle, an obtuse-angled triangle has an obtuse angle, and an acute-angled triangle has three acute angles.
G.81 (II.def.1): Any rectangular parallelogram is said to becontained by the twosegments containing theright angle.
G.96 (I.def.18): A semicircle is the figure contained by a diameter and the arc cut off by it.
G.98 (III.1): Find the center of a given circle.
G.102 (III.5): If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same center.
G.108 (III.10): A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.
G.111 (III.def.2): Asegment is said totouch a circle which, meeting thecircle and being produced, does not cut the circle.
G.117 (III.def.7): Anangle of a segment is that contained by asegment and a arc of acircle.
G.118 (III.16): The segment drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the segment and the arc another segment ca...
G.120 (III.18): If a segment touch a circle, and a segment be joined from the center to the point of contact, the segment so joined is perpendicular to the tangent.
G.122 (III.def.10): Asector of a circle is thefigure which, when anangle is constructed at thecenter of thecircle, is contained by thesegments containing the angle and the arc cut off by them.
G.123 (III.20): In a circle the angle at the center is double of the angle at the arc, when the angles have the same arc as base.
G.124 (III.21): In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal.
G.125 (III.22): The opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles.
G.126 (III.def.6): Asegment of a circle is thefigure contained by asegment and a arc of acircle.
G.127 (III.def.11): Similar segments of circles are those which admit equalangles, or in which the angles are equal.
G.129 (III.24): Similar segments of circles on equal segments are equal.
G.131 (III.def.1): Equal circles are those thediameters of which are equal, or the radii of which are equal.
G.132 (III.def.9): And, when thesegments containing theangle cut off a arc, the angle is said tostand upon that arc.
G.133 (III.26): In equal circles equal angles stand on equal arcs, whether they stand at the centres or at the arcs.
G.134 (III.27): In equal circles angles standing on equal arcs are equal, whether they stand at the centres or at the arcs.

G.139 (III.31): In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of...
G.148 (IV.def.3): Apolygon is said to beinscribed in a circle when eachangle of the inscribedfigure lies on the arc of thecircle.
G.150 (IV.def.4): Apolygon is said to becircumscribed about a circle, when each side of the circumscribedfigure touches the arc of thecircle.
G.158 (IV.6): Inscribe in a given circle a square.
G.159 (IV.7): Circumscribe about a given circle a square.
G.169 (V.def.1): A magnitude is apart of a magnitude, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater.
G.170 (V.def.2): The greater is amultiple of the less when it ismeasured by the less.

G.173 (V.def.3): Aratio is a sort of relation in respect of size between two magnitudes of the same kind.

G.180 (V.def.6): Let magnitudes which have thesame ratio be calledproportional.
G.181 (V.def.11): The termcorresponding magnitudes is used of antecedents in relation to antecedents, and of consequents in relation to consequents.
G.182 (V.def.13): Inverse ratio means taking theconsequent as antecedent in relation to the antecedent as consequent.
G.183 (V.7): Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio, as also has the same to equal magnitudes.
G.184 (V.def.4): Magnitudes are said tohave a ratio to one another which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another.

G.186 (V.8): Of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has; and the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater.
G.187 (V.9): Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal; and magnitudes to which the same has the same ratio are equal.
G.188 (V.10): Of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less.
G.189 (V.11): Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another.
G.190 (V.12): If any number of magnitudes be proportional, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so will all the antecedents be to all the consequents.

G.193 (V.15): Parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order.
G.194 (V.def.12): Alternate ratio means taking theantecedent in relation to the antecedent and the consequent in relation to the consequent.
G.195 (V.16): If four magnitudes be proportional, they is proportional alternately.
G.196 (V.def.14): Composition of a ratio means taking theantecedent together with the consequent as one in relation to the consequent by itself.
G.197 (V.def.15): Separation of a ratio means taking the excess by which theantecedent exceeds the consequent in relation to the consequent by itself.
G.198 (V.17): If magnitudes be proportional componendo, they is proportional separando.
G.199 (V.18): If magnitudes be proportional separando, they is proportional componendo.

G.205 (V.22): If there be any number of magnitudes whatever, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two together are in the same ratio, they is in the same ratio ex aequali.
G.209 (VI.def.4): The height of anyfigure is theperpendicular drawn from the vertex to the base.
G.210 (VI.1): Triangles and parallelograms which are under the same height are to one another as their bases.
G.211 (VI.2): If a segment be drawn parallel to one of the sides of a triangle, it will cut the sides of the triangle proportionally; and, if the sides of the triangle be cut proportionally, the...
G.213 (VI.4): In equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, and those are corresponding sides which subtend the equal angles.

G.217 (VI.def.1): Similar polygons are such as have theirangles severally equal and the sides about the equal anglesproportional.
G.221 (VI.11): To two given segments to find a third proportional.
G.222 (VI.12): To three given segments to find a fourth proportional.
G.224 (VI.def.2): Reciprocally related figures have their sides about equal angles reciprocally proportional.

G.229 (VI.18): Describe on a given segment a rectilinear figure similar and similarly situated to a given rectilinear figure.
G.230 (V.def.9): When three magnitudes areproportional, the first is said to have to the third theduplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.
G.231 (VI.19): Similar triangles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of the corresponding sides.
G.232 (VI.20): Similar polygons are divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon has to the polygon a ratio duplicate...

G.247 (VII.def.1): Anunit is that by virtue of which each of the things that exist is called one.
G.248 (VII.def.2): Anumber is a multitude composed ofunits.
G.253 (VII.def.3): Anumber is apart of a number, the less of the greater, when itmeasures the greater;
G.256 (VII.def.5): The greaternumber is amultiple of the less when it ismeasured by the less.
G.269 (VII.def.15): Anumber is said tomultiply a number when that which is multiplied is added to itself as many times as there areunits in the other, and thus some number is produced.
G.302 (VII.def.6): Aneven number is that which is divisible into two equal parts.

G.502 (XI.1): A part of a segment cannot be in the plane of reference and a part in a plane more elevated.
G.503 (XI.2): If two segments cut one another, they are in one plane, and every triangle is in one plane.
G.504 (XI.3): If two planes cut one another, their common section is a segment.
G.505 (XI.def.3): Asegment isat right angles to a plane, when it makesright angles with all the segments which meet it and are in theplane.
G.506 (XI.4): If a segment be set up at right angles to two segments which cut one another, at their common point of section, it is at right angles to the plane through them.
G.507 (XI.5): If a segment be set up at right angles to three segments which meet one another, at their common point of section, the three segments are in one plane.
G.508 (XI.6): If two segments be at right angles to the same plane, the segments is parallel.
G.509 (XI.7): If two segments be parallel and points be taken at random on each of them, the segment joining the points is in the same plane with the parallel lines.
G.510 (XI.8): If two segments be parallel, and one of them be at right angles to any plane, the remaining one is at right angles to the same plane.
G.511 (XI.9): Straight lines which are parallel to the same segment and are not in the same plane with it are also parallel to one another.
G.512 (XI.10): If two segments meeting one another be parallel to two segments meeting one another not in the same plane, they will contain equal angles.
G.516 (XI.def.8): Parallel planes are those which do not meet.
G.519 (XI.16): If two parallel planes be cut by any plane, their common sections are parallel.
G.529 (XI.def.1): Asolid is that which has length, breadth, and depth.
G.530 (XI.24): If a solid be contained by parallel planes, the opposite planes in it are equal and parallelogrammic.
G.531 (XI.25): If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane which is parallel to the opposite planes, then, as the base is to the base, so will the solid be to the solid.
G.533 (XI.def.2): Anextremity of asolid is asurface.
G.535 (XI.def.10): Equal and similar solid figures are thosecontained by similar planes equal in multitude and in magnitude.
G.537 (XI.def.13): Aprism is asolid figure contained byplanes two of which, namely those which are opposite, are equal, similar andparallel, while the rest are parallelograms.
G.538 (XI.28): If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane through the diagonals of the opposite planes, the solid is bisected by the plane.
G.539 (XI.29): Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are on the same segments, are equal.
G.540 (XI.30): Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are not on the same segments, are equal.
G.541 (XI.31): Parallelepipedal solids which are on equal bases and of the same height are equal.
G.542 (XI.32): Parallelepipedal solids which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.
G.550 (XI.39): If there be two prisms of equal height, and one have a parallelogram as base and the other a triangle, and if the parallelogram be double of the triangle, the prisms is equal.
G.551 (XII.1): Similar polygons inscribed in circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.
G.552 (XII.2): Circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.
G.553 (XI.def.12): Apyramid is asolid figure, contained byplanes, which is constructed from one plane to onepoint.

G.556 (XII.5): Pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as the bases.
G.557 (XII.6): Pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases.
G.558 (XII.7): Any prism which has a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another which have triangular bases.

G.563 (XII.10): Any cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height.
